idiom_name: Unity GameObject with AddComponent<T>/GetComponent<T> components (or plain IComponent slots)
implementation_notes: The dominant .NET realization is a game-engine container: Unity documents the GameObject as 'a container for functional components', components are MonoBehaviour subclasses attached with AddComponent<T>() and retrieved with GetComponent<T>(), and Godot's C# nodes compose the same way - the container type, the component base class and the assembly API all come from the framework, so almost no glue is hand-written. Engine-free code writes the same structure by hand as an interface plus List<IComponent> (the .NET component model in System.ComponentModel - IComponent/IContainer/ISite - is the framework's older, design-time reading of containment and does not compose behaviour).
pitfalls: GetComponent<T>()/OfType<T>() returns null (or a default) when the component was never attached, so a missing capability is a NullReferenceException at runtime rather than a compile error.
Removing a component is deferred (Unity requires Object.Destroy and applies it at end of frame), so a component list can change after your loop has decided it is up to date.

Unity's MonoBehaviour lifecycle (Awake/Start/Update/OnDestroy) is ordered by the engine, not by your code, and components cannot be constructed with arguments - pass configuration through fields or a Configure call.

variants.name: Plain .NET entity with interface components and a component list
variants.idiom_name: List<IComponent> plus generic Get<T>() lookups; no engine required
variants.implementation_notes: Without an engine you write the container yourself: an interface with one Update hook, a list on the entity, generic accessors for retrieval and a builder/factory that assembles each entity kind. This keeps the pattern usable in server-side or desktop code where a game engine would be absurd, and it makes required components explicit (validate the assembled list in the factory) instead of relying on engine lookup failures.
pitfalls: OfType<T>() allocates and scans the whole list on every lookup; cache the typed handle at assembly time on the hot path.
Nothing prevents two components of the same type from being added, and both will update - enforce one instance per type in Add().
Generic variance: Get<T>() returning a base interface makes it easy to call behaviour a component does not own; keep the component contract narrow.
